To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

ECDSA is provably insecure if a few bits (about log1/2p) of the random nonce are known for a linear number of ECDSA signatures, and that the number of bits required can be reduced to about log log p with a subexponential running time, and to two in polynomial-time if an oracle for the closest vector problem for lattices in the infinity norm is available.

ECDSA is not secure if a few bits of k are known, that the number of known bits can be reduced to two with ideal lattice techniques, and that the security of ECDSA is not provable in the random oracle model.

(i) if a few bits of the nonces are partially known for a number at most linear in the bit size of the curve order, then ECDSA is broken with polynomial-time algorithms; (ii) if a few more bits of the nonce are partially known, then ECDSA can be broken in subexponential time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: how many bits of k are required to recover DSA/ECDSA keys in polynomial time, and how many bits are sufficient in subexponential time?

the security of ECDSA against the so-called partial key exposure attacks, where the attacker is allowed to know a few bits of the random number k used in each signature generation, for a certain number of signatures.

the following three problems: (1) the insecurity of DSA when a few bits of the random nonce k are known; (2) the insecurity of ECDSA when a few bits (or even one bit) of the random nonce r are known; and (3) the insecurity of both DSA and ECDSA when a small part of the random nonce is known, and this part is not known to be random.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ECDSA signature algorithm is not secure when a few consecutive nonces are known, and that this insecurity is even worse than that of DSA.
ECDSA, as well as the standard DSA algorithm, are not safe when a few consecutive random bits are leaked.
ECDSA is provably insecure with respect to nonce leakage, unless the hash function used is a pseudorandom generator (which is not a realistic assumption).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ECDSA with partially known nonces is insecure, and that the security of the DSA variant with random nonces is only slightly better than that of ECDSA.

ECDSA is provably insecure with a partially known nonce, even with the best possible partial knowledge, unless the underlying elliptic curve group is a very large prime-order subgroup of a large finite field.

, for any fixed positive integer t, the secret ECDSA key can be recovered from a number of ECDSA signatures at most O(log q/t) and t known consecutive bits of the nonces used in these signatures, with a running time of the form qO(1/t).
The main takeaway from our work is that

the security of ECDSA is much weaker than that of DSA, and in fact, ECDSA is provably broken in the case where a single bit of k is known, for any number of signatures, even when the hash function is modeled as random.

the security of both DSA and ECDSA can be broken in polynomial time if a few bits of the nonces are known, and that this is not an artifact of the particular attack method, but rather a fundamental property of these signature algorithms.
ECDSA is not more secure than DSA against such attacks.
